questions.stem: Diffraction of a wave is best described as the

options.text: bouncing back of the wave from a barrier
change in speed of the wave as it enters a new medium
spreading out of the wave as it passes through a narrow gap or round an obstacle
cancellation of two waves that arrive out of phase

questions.explanation: Diffraction is the bending and spreading of wavefronts at the edges of an obstacle or aperture. The frequency, wavelength and speed all stay the same; only the shape of the wavefront changes as it opens out beyond the gap.

distractorRationale.a: That is reflection
distractorRationale.d: That is destructive interference

questions.stem: For a steady interference pattern to be observed, the two sources must be

options.text: coherent, with the same frequency and a constant phase relationship
placed far apart compared with the wavelength

questions.explanation: If the frequencies differ or the phase relationship drifts, the points of reinforcement and cancellation move about and the pattern is washed out. Coherent sources keep the path-difference condition fixed at every point, so the bright and dark regions stay put.

distractorRationale.a: Different frequencies give a constantly shifting pattern rather than a steady one
distractorRationale.c: Very unequal amplitudes give poor contrast, but the real requirement is coherence
distractorRationale.d: Wide separation actually makes the fringes narrower and harder to observe

questions.stem: When a wave is reflected from a plane barrier, which of its properties changes?
questions.explanation: The wave stays in the same medium after reflection, so its speed is unchanged, and the source still vibrates at the same rate, so its frequency is unchanged. With both fixed, $v = f\lambda$ requires the wavelength to be unchanged too. Only the direction of travel is altered.

distractorRationale.a: Frequency is set by the source and reflection does not alter it
distractorRationale.b: Wavelength depends on speed and frequency, both of which are unchanged
distractorRationale.c: Speed depends on the medium, which is the same before and after reflection

questions.stem: Diffraction of waves at a gap is most pronounced when the width of the gap is

options.text: very much larger than the wavelength
very much smaller than the amplitude
exactly equal to the period of the wave

questions.explanation: When the gap and the wavelength are of similar size the emerging wavefronts spread out almost as a semicircle. A gap far wider than the wavelength lets the wave through nearly unchanged, with only slight spreading at the edges.

distractorRationale.a: A very wide gap gives almost no observable spreading, which is why light casts sharp shadows
distractorRationale.c: Amplitude has no bearing on how much a wave diffracts
distractorRationale.d: Period is a time and a gap width is a length, so they cannot be compared

questions.stem: A student can hear a teacher speaking through an open doorway but cannot see her. This is because

options.text: the wavelength of sound is comparable to the width of the doorway while that of light is far smaller
light cannot be diffracted at all
sound does not obey the laws of reflection

questions.explanation: Speech has a wavelength of about a metre, similar to the width of a doorway, so it diffracts strongly and spreads round the frame. Visible light has a wavelength of a fraction of a micrometre, utterly tiny compared with the doorway, so it barely spreads and travels on in almost straight lines.

distractorRationale.a: Light travels roughly a million times faster than sound, so this is factually reversed
distractorRationale.c: Light does diffract, but the effect is only detectable at gaps comparable to its very short wavelength
distractorRationale.d: Sound obeys the laws of reflection perfectly well — that is how echoes arise

questions.stem: Two coherent sources emit waves of wavelength λ. Destructive interference occurs at a point where the path difference is
questions.explanation: A path difference of an odd number of half-wavelengths puts the two waves exactly out of phase, so a crest from one meets a trough from the other and they cancel. Writing this as $\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$ covers 0.5λ, 1.5λ, 2.5λ and so on.

distractorRationale.a: A whole number of wavelengths gives constructive interference, not destructive
distractorRationale.c: Dividing by n has no physical basis and would not give a phase reversal
distractorRationale.d: Squaring the wavelength gives an area, which cannot equal a path difference

questions.stem: Two coherent loudspeakers emit sound of wavelength 0.50 m. Calculate the smallest non-zero path difference at which a quiet point (destructive interference) occurs. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: Destructive interference needs a path difference of $\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$. The smallest such value takes $n = 0$, giving $\frac{\lambda}{2} = \frac{0.50}{2} = 0.25\ \text{m}$. At that path difference a crest from one speaker meets a trough from the other.

questions.stem: A wave passes from a medium in which it travels quickly into one in which it travels more slowly, striking the boundary at an angle. The wave will bend

options.text: towards the normal, and its wavelength will decrease
away from the normal, and its wavelength will increase
towards the normal, and its frequency will decrease
away from the normal, and its frequency will increase

questions.explanation: Entering a slower medium makes the wave bend towards the normal. The frequency is fixed by the source, so from $v = f\lambda$ a smaller speed must mean a shorter wavelength. Frequency never changes on refraction.

distractorRationale.b: Bending away from the normal and lengthening the wavelength happens when the wave speeds up, not slows down
distractorRationale.c: The bending direction is right but the frequency does not change on refraction
distractorRationale.d: Both the bending direction and the claim about frequency are wrong

questions.stem: A standing wave is set up on a stretched string vibrating at 100 Hz. Adjacent nodes are found to be 0.30 m apart. Calculate the speed of the waves on the string. Give your answer in metres per second.
questions.explanation: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so $\frac{\lambda}{2} = 0.30\ \text{m}$ and $\lambda = 0.60\ \text{m}$. Then $v = f\lambda = 100 \times 0.60 = 60\ \text{m/s}$. Taking 0.30 m as the full wavelength would halve the answer.

questions.stem: Which pair of phenomena provides evidence that light travels as a wave?
questions.explanation: Streams of particles can reflect off surfaces and change direction at boundaries, so reflection and refraction do not settle the question. Only waves can reinforce and cancel one another or spread round an obstacle, so interference and diffraction are the decisive evidence for the wave nature of light.

distractorRationale.a: Particles bounce off surfaces and travel in straight lines too, so neither is evidence of wave behaviour
distractorRationale.c: Newton explained both with a particle model, so they cannot distinguish the two theories
distractorRationale.d: Straight-line travel and sharp shadows were historically used to argue that light is a stream of particles

questions.stem: When a wave passes from one medium to another, the change in speed leads to a change in its direction. This phenomenon is known as:
questions.explanation: Refraction occurs when a wave enters a medium at an angle, causing it to change speed and direction. This effect is commonly observed with light waves as they pass through different materials.

distractorRationale.a: Reflection involves bouncing back of waves, not a change in direction due to speed.
distractorRationale.c: Diffraction refers to the bending of waves around obstacles, not their change in speed.
distractorRationale.d: Interference is the superposition of waves, not related to the change of medium.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes constructive interference?

options.text: Waves combine to form a larger amplitude

questions.explanation: Constructive interference occurs when two waves meet in phase, resulting in a wave with a greater amplitude. This is a fundamental principle in wave behavior.

distractorRationale.a: That describes destructive interference, not constructive.
distractorRationale.c: The direction of travel does not define constructive interference.
distractorRationale.d: Reflection is a separate phenomenon from interference.

questions.stem: What is the primary condition necessary for diffraction to be most apparent?

options.text: The wavelength of the wave is much smaller than the obstacle
The wavelength of the wave is approximately equal to the size of the obstacle
The speed of the wave is constant
The amplitude of the wave is minimized

questions.explanation: Diffraction is most pronounced when the wavelength of the wave is comparable to the dimensions of the obstacle or aperture. This allows the wave to bend around the edges effectively.

distractorRationale.a: When the wavelength is much smaller, diffraction is minimal.
distractorRationale.c: Constant speed does not influence the extent of diffraction.
distractorRationale.d: Amplitude does not directly affect diffraction visibility.

questions.stem: If a wave reflects off a surface, which of the following properties remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: When a wave reflects off a surface, its frequency remains unchanged. The speed and wavelength may change depending on the medium, but frequency is determined by the source.

distractorRationale.b: Wavelength can change if the wave enters a different medium.
distractorRationale.c: Speed can change with different media.
distractorRationale.d: Amplitude can change depending on the reflecting surface.

questions.stem: Which phenomenon demonstrates the wave nature of sound when it bends around a barrier?
questions.explanation: Diffraction is the bending of waves around obstacles and openings. This property is particularly observable in sound waves, allowing them to be heard even when the source is not directly visible.

distractorRationale.a: Reflection involves bouncing off surfaces, not bending.
distractorRationale.b: Refraction involves a change in speed and direction, not bending around barriers.
distractorRationale.d: Interference involves the superposition of waves, not their bending.

questions.stem: In a standing wave, the points of maximum amplitude are known as:
questions.explanation: In a standing wave, antinodes are the points where the amplitude is at its maximum, while nodes are points of zero amplitude. This creates a characteristic pattern in standing waves.

distractorRationale.a: Nodes are points of zero amplitude, not maximum.
distractorRationale.c: Waves refer to the overall phenomenon, not specific points.
distractorRationale.d: Crests refer to peaks in a traveling wave, not specifically in standing waves.

questions.stem: What happens to the wavelength of a wave when its frequency increases, assuming the speed remains constant?
questions.explanation: According to the wave equation (v = fλ), if the speed (v) is constant and frequency (f) increases, the wavelength (λ) must decrease. This is an essential relationship in wave behavior.

distractorRationale.a: An increase in frequency leads to a decrease in wavelength.
distractorRationale.c: Wavelength cannot remain the same if frequency changes.
distractorRationale.d: Doubling of wavelength is not a consequence of increasing frequency.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about sound waves is true?

options.text: They can travel through a vacuum.
They travel faster in air than in water.
They have a fixed speed regardless of medium.

questions.explanation: Sound waves are longitudinal waves, meaning the particle displacement is parallel to the direction of wave propagation. This is a fundamental characteristic of sound.

distractorRationale.a: Sound requires a medium to travel and cannot propagate through a vacuum.
distractorRationale.c: Sound travels faster in water than in air due to the denser medium.
distractorRationale.d: The speed of sound varies with the medium through which it travels.

questions.stem: In a double-slit experiment, the pattern formed on the screen is a result of:
questions.explanation: The double-slit experiment demonstrates interference, where waves from two slits combine to form a pattern of alternating bright and dark fringes on a screen. This is a classic demonstration of wave behavior.

distractorRationale.a: Reflection does not create the pattern observed in this experiment.
distractorRationale.b: Refraction refers to bending of waves, not the interference pattern.
distractorRationale.d: While diffraction occurs, the specific pattern is due to interference.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the term 'node' in wave theory?
questions.explanation: A node is a point in a standing wave where the amplitude is minimum, resulting in no displacement of the medium at that point. This is crucial in understanding standing waves.

distractorRationale.a: That describes an antinode, not a node.
distractorRationale.c: Reflection does not define a node in wave theory.
distractorRationale.d: Refraction is unrelated to the definition of a node.

questions.stem: What is the effect of increasing the amplitude of a wave?
questions.explanation: Increasing the amplitude of a wave results in a louder sound in the case of sound waves, as amplitude is directly related to the energy and intensity of the wave.

distractorRationale.a: Amplitude does not directly affect frequency.
distractorRationale.b: Wavelength is determined by frequency and speed, not amplitude.
distractorRationale.d: Speed is determined by the medium, not amplitude.

questions.stem: When a wave is refracted, which of the following properties changes?
questions.explanation: Refraction occurs when a wave passes from one medium to another, leading to a change in speed. As the wave changes speed, its wavelength also changes, but its frequency remains constant.

distractorRationale.a: Wavelength does change, but it is a consequence of the change in speed.
distractorRationale.d: Amplitude does not necessarily change during refraction.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the phenomenon of reflection?

options.text: Change of direction at a boundary
Combining of waves to form a new wave
Separation of waves into different colors

questions.explanation: Reflection is the change of direction of a wave when it encounters a boundary or surface, returning it to the original medium. This principle is fundamental in understanding wave behavior.

distractorRationale.a: This describes diffraction, not reflection.
distractorRationale.c: This describes interference, not reflection.
distractorRationale.d: This describes dispersion, not reflection.

questions.stem: In the context of sound waves, what is meant by 'destructive interference'?
questions.explanation: Destructive interference occurs when two waves meet in such a way that their crests and troughs align oppositely, effectively canceling each other out and resulting in reduced amplitude.

distractorRationale.a: This describes constructive interference.
distractorRationale.c: This is unrelated to the concept of interference.
distractorRationale.d: This describes reflection, not interference.

questions.stem: What is the primary effect of increasing the wavelength of a wave while keeping its speed constant?
questions.explanation: When the speed of a wave is constant, an increase in wavelength results in a decrease in frequency, according to the wave equation (speed = frequency × wavelength).

distractorRationale.a: This is incorrect; frequency decreases with increased wavelength.
distractorRationale.c: Amplitude is independent of wavelength in this context.
distractorRationale.d: Frequency does change with wavelength when speed is constant.

options.text: The wavelength is much smaller than the obstacle
The wavelength is comparable to the size of the obstacle

questions.explanation: Diffraction is most pronounced when the wavelength of the wave is comparable to the size of the obstacle or aperture it encounters, allowing the wave to bend around it significantly.

distractorRationale.a: This would result in minimal diffraction.
distractorRationale.c: Wave speed does not directly affect the degree of diffraction.

distractorRationale.a: Antinodes are points of maximum displacement.
distractorRationale.c: Crests are the high points of a wave.

Waves change direction at a boundary

questions.stem: When two waves meet and their amplitudes add together, resulting in a larger amplitude, this phenomenon is known as:

distractorRationale.a: Destructive interference occurs when waves meet out of phase, canceling each other out.
distractorRationale.c: Diffraction refers to the bending of waves around obstacles, not the addition of amplitudes.
distractorRationale.d: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another, not related to amplitude.
